Copycat Dunkin Cake Munchkins (Made at Home)

ByNellie
6 shares
  • Share
  • Tweet
  • LinkedIn
Jump to Recipe
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:07
Instaread

I’m old enough to remember when Munchkins were introduced, and I remember exactly how I felt about it — like Dunkin had figured out that the best part of a donut was always the first bite, and they’d found a way to make the whole thing be that.

I was working a corporate job when I first brought a box of them into the office. Ten-pack becomes a hundred-pack when you’re in a conference room, and I walked in with that pink box like I’d done something. I was absolutely the star of that morning. Nobody talked about anything else until the box was empty.

That was over fifteen years ago. Now my kids are the ones requesting Dunkin, and we grab a ten-pack whenever we’re anywhere near one — which in New York is approximately always. But being able to make them at home means the box is bigger, the price is lower, and nobody has to agree on what else to order.

These are fried doughnut holes dipped in a vanilla glaze while they’re still warm. The glaze sets as they cool on the rack and you end up with exactly what you’re picturing. Make them fast and eat them warm — that’s when they’re closest to the real thing.

What You Need

For the doughnut holes:

  • 2 cups all-purpose flour
  • 2 tablespoons granulated sugar
  • 4½ teaspoons baking powder (see note below)
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • 1 cup milk
  • 1 egg
  • ¼ cup unsalted butter, melted
  • Oil for frying

For the glaze:

  • 2 cups powdered sugar
  • 2 tablespoons milk
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

Equipment: Large pot or deep pan for frying, 1-inch cookie scoop, cooling rack, baking sheet, parchment paper, paper towels

Ingredient Notes

Flour: All-purpose, measured by spooning into the cup and leveling — not scooping directly from the bag, which packs it and adds more flour than intended.

Baking powder: The leavening that gives these their light interior. Measure carefully.

Butter: Melted and slightly cooled before it goes into the batter. Very hot butter added directly can start cooking the egg when they’re combined.

Oil: Use a neutral, high smoke-point oil — vegetable, canola, or peanut. Fill the pot to at least 2-3 inches deep so the doughnut holes can float freely rather than sitting on the bottom and cooking unevenly.

Glaze: Simple powdered sugar glaze — make this first so it’s ready to go the moment the doughnut holes come out. The glaze adheres best when the doughnut holes are still slightly warm.

How to Make Them

Step 1: Make the glaze first
Whisk together the powdered sugar, milk, and vanilla extract until completely smooth with no lumps. Set aside — you’ll want this ready the moment the doughnut holes are done frying.

Step 2: Mix the wet ingredients
In a medium bowl, whisk together the milk and egg until combined.

Step 3: Mix the dry ingredients
In a separate large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.

Step 4: Combine
Pour the milk and egg mixture into the dry ingredients along with the melted butter. Mix until a soft dough comes together. Don’t overmix — stop when no dry flour is visible.

Step 5: Heat the oil
Heat about 3 inches of oil in a large pot or deep pan to 350°F. If you don’t have a thermometer, test with a small piece of dough — it should sizzle immediately and float to the surface. If it sinks and sits, the oil isn’t hot enough. If it browns in under a minute, the oil is too hot.

Step 6: Scoop and fry
Using a 1-inch scoop, drop dough balls into the hot oil one at a time. Don’t overcrowd — work in batches of 6-8, leaving space for them to move freely. Fry for about 2 minutes, turning with a spoon so they brown evenly on all sides, until golden brown all over.

Step 7: Drain
Transfer the fried doughnut holes to a plate lined with paper towels to drain excess oil for about a minute.

Step 8: Glaze
While still slightly warm, dip each doughnut hole into the glaze, coating all sides. Place on a parchment-lined cooling rack — the excess glaze will drip off and the coating will set as they cool.

Step 9: Serve warm
These are at their best within 20-30 minutes of glazing, while the exterior is set but the interior is still soft.

Tips for Getting These Right

Oil temperature is the whole game. Too cool and the doughnut holes absorb oil instead of forming a crust — they’ll be greasy and dense. Too hot and they brown on the outside before the center cooks through. A thermometer is worth using here. If you don’t have one, the small-piece-of-dough test described above is reliable.

Work in batches. Adding too many doughnut holes at once drops the oil temperature immediately and you lose the crust effect. Six to eight at a time maximum depending on your pot size.

Glaze while warm, not hot. Dipping a very hot doughnut hole into glaze causes the glaze to slide right off. Thirty seconds on the paper towel is enough — you want warm, not steaming.

Eat them the same day. These are genuinely at their peak warm and fresh. Day-two doughnut holes are still edible but they lose the crisp-to-soft contrast that makes the first batch so good. Make what you’ll eat.

Variations

Cinnamon sugar: Skip the glaze entirely and roll warm doughnut holes in a mixture of ½ cup granulated sugar and 1 tablespoon cinnamon. This is actually the faster version and most people argue it’s better.

Chocolate glaze: Replace the vanilla glaze with a chocolate version — melt ½ cup semi-sweet chocolate chips with 2 tablespoons of heavy cream, stir until smooth, and dip as usual.

Sprinkles: Add sprinkles to the glaze immediately after dipping, before it sets, for a birthday-party version that kids will absolutely lose their minds about.

FAQs

Can I bake these instead of frying?

Not with this recipe — the dough is specifically developed for frying, and baking it would produce a dense, heavy result rather than a light doughnut hole. If you want a baked version, a different dough (closer to a muffin batter) would be needed.

Can I make the dough ahead of time?

The dough can be mixed and refrigerated for up to an hour before frying. Beyond that, the baking powder continues to activate and the leavening effect diminishes. Fry as close to mixing as practical.

Why are my doughnut holes greasy?

The oil temperature was too low. The dough needs to hit hot oil to immediately form a crust — when the oil is too cool, the dough absorbs it instead. Let the oil come back to 350°F between batches.

Why are they raw in the middle?

The oil was too hot. The outside browned before the center had time to cook through. Lower the temperature slightly and give each batch a few extra seconds.

How many does this make?

About 24 doughnut holes using a 1-inch scoop.

The intro to this post tells the whole story — Munchkins have been a fixture in my life for decades, and making a batch at home that my kids actually ask for is the full circle moment. Make them while the oil is hot and eat them while the glaze is still setting. Leave a comment if you went the cinnamon sugar route instead — that debate has no wrong answer.

Yield: 24 munchkins

Copycat Dunkin Cake Munchkins (Made at Home)

Prep Time: 20 minutes
Cook Time: 6 minutes
Total Time: 6 minutes

Homemade copycat Dunkin Cake Munchkins — fried doughnut holes dipped in a vanilla glaze while still warm, with a crisp glazed exterior and a soft, pillowy center. Twenty-four doughnut holes from one batch, ready in under 30 minutes, and significantly better than anything sitting in a drive-through case.

No Ratings

Ingredients

  • Doughnut Hole Batter
  • 1 cup milk
  • 1 egg
  • 2 cups all purpose flour
  • 2 tablespoons white granulated sugar
  • 4 ½ tablespoons baking powder
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • ¼ cup unsalted butter, melted
  • Glaze
  • 2 cups powdered sugar
  • 2 tablespoons milk
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

Instructions

    1. First make the glaze. In a mixing bowl add the powdered sugar, milk and vanilla extract and whisk together. Set aside
    2. While that heats up, whisk together the milk and egg in a bowl.
    3. In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt.
    4. Pour the milk mixture into the dry ingredients, as well as the melted butter.
    5. Mix together until a soft dough forms.
    6. Use a 1 inch scooper to scoop the dough balls into the hot oil. Be sure not to overcrowd the pot/pan.
    7. Use a spoon to turn over the donut holes cooking until golden brown on all sides, about 2 minutes of cooking.
    8. Prepare a cooling rack with a baking sheet with parchment paper underneath.
    9. Transfer to a plate covered with a paper towel to let the excess oil drip off.
    10. Once the doughnuts have cooled slightly, dip each doughnut hole into the glaze and place on the prepared cooking rack. This will allow the excess glaze to drip off and the glaze to cool.
    11. Serve while still warm!

Nutrition Information

Yield

24

Serving Size

1
